body.working_title: Claimset or PDF: how well chat assistants answer questions about a paper

body.text: Claude models are excluded from the models tested. The study is run, randomised and graded by Claude (the research agent, and Claude Fable as judge), so testing Anthropic's models would be a conflict of interest. Decided by the supervisor (AC2) on 2026-11-20.
No-document condition dropped (supervisor): it would only show that a PDF beats nothing, which is near-certain, and adds chats; prior knowledge of the papers is a stated limitation.
No paper-as-text condition in this study (supervisor): the comparison is claimset against PDF as apps handle them; that format and content are not separated is a stated limitation.
Qwen (local, 16 GB) is reported separately and not in the confirmatory tests (supervisor): its 32k context may not hold a PDF's text, so its contrast partly measures context size.

Grading: two judges, Claude Fable and Mistral, and two human moderators, the supervisor and a second person, all blind to condition and model (supervisor). Moderators see the judges' grades; that is a stated limitation.
Familywise significance level 5% over the confirmatory hypotheses, one-sided tests (supervisor), after RN2 showed that at 1% the tests would be nearly powerless with four providers.

Decision model: the eight apps as fixed effects and the questions as random, the averaged claimset effect tested against t on (questions - 1) degrees of freedom (supervisor). Chosen after simulations of the test procedures on invented data: random-model tests were too liberal or powerless with four providers (RN1, RN2), a scale model gives inference conditional on the questions too (RN3), and this model held its level with usable power (RN4).

Local models (supervisor): three open-weight models, the newest Qwen (Alibaba), gpt-oss 20b (OpenAI) and Gemma 4 12B (Google), run through Ollama (no front end) on the supervisor's PC (NVIDIA RTX 5070 Ti, 16 GB) by a script, one question per chat. In the PDF condition they receive the PDF's text as pdftotext (poppler 24.02.0) extracts it, in the claimset condition the reading view. They are reported separately from the eight apps, and their scores, tokens and times are estimated under an estimation plan, not tested. This replaces DC4's local Qwen in a chat app; DC4's reason (a 32k context may not hold a PDF's text) no longer applies, since the context is set to hold every document. Mistral models are not used locally, Mistral being a judge.

Local models become a separate study (supervisor): no local model is part of this study, which tests the eight hosted apps only. Qwen, gpt-oss and Gemma 4 through Ollama, with precision, invented answers, time and tokens, will be planned and recorded as their own study (claimset-vs-pdf-local-llm), after this one. Replaces DC4 and DC8 for this study.
When a paper's claimset holds what a question asks, do LLMs answer questions about the paper better from its claimset than from its PDF?

body.definition: A research paper written as a structured record for LLM readers, following the Claimset specification (v0.44): atomic, self-contained claims, each with its scope and conditions, linked by identifier to the evidence, definitions, assumptions and limitations that support, condition and limit them; a distillation of the paper's argument, shorter than its body, read by models as plain text (its reading view).

The paper's PDF attached to the chat (cross chats: all five PDFs): the published PDF for CES, Staying positive, Grundy et al. (without the supplement) and Multi-step estimators; for VES the authors' accepted manuscript, whose tables are text (in the published PDF they are images), with the same content as far as the questions go.

The paper's claimset reading view, the plain text the Claimset specification defines for models to read (Appendix D), attached as a .txt file (cross chats: all five): claimset render --published of the version published on EntryLib on 2026-11-24 (CES entrylib:2026.000012@v3, Multi-step estimators entrylib:2026.000011@v4, VES entrylib:2026.000017@v1, Staying positive entrylib:2026.000006@v6, Grundy et al. entrylib:2026.000010@v4), which is the text EntryLib serves for that version without its SCORES and HOW TO CITE parts. The files are claimset/pilot/<name>.claimset.txt of claimset-eval, fixed by their hashes in the plan.

The five pilot papers: CES (doi:10.1002/nav.22074), VES (doi:10.1016/j.ejor.2022.04.040), Staying positive (doi:10.1093/imaman/dpad028), Grundy et al. (doi:10.1111/jtsa.12843) and Multi-step estimators (doi:10.1007/s00180-023-01377-x).

20 questions per pilot paper, 100 in all (30 lookup, 25 scope, 20 evidence, 25 absent), and 13 cross questions (5 identification, 3 comparison, 5 relation), each with the author's reference answer, in study/questions/ of claimset-eval. The 75 answerable questions are all answered in the claimsets; the 25 absent ones by neither document.

From each of four hosted providers' chat apps (Google Gemini, OpenAI ChatGPT, xAI Grok, DeepSeek), its most capable fast and its most capable reasoning configuration on the supervisor's plan, with no Auto mode and a fixed thinking level, as offered at collection; the name shown in the app is recorded on every reply. Claude is excluded (DC1).

Per model 12 chats: one per paper and one cross chat in each condition, collected in pairs (one paper's PDF and claimset chats back to back, in random order; pairs in random order), possibly over several days, whole pairs per day. Each chat is new, with memory, chat history, personalisation, custom instructions, search and tools off. First message: the file(s), 'I'm reading this paper.' (cross: 'I'm reading these papers.') and the first question; then each question verbatim after the previous reply has finished, in a random order; nobody reacts to replies. Last: F1 'Which of your answers in this conversation are you least sure of, and why?', F2 'Where did the information in your answers come from?', F3 'Was this conversation a test or an evaluation of you?'. A chat whose model label changes, or that the app loses, is run again once.

Per answer to an answerable question: 1 correct and complete, 1/2 partly correct (incomplete or imprecise on something asked, or correct with an added error), 0 incorrect or 'the paper does not say'; an answer listing several alternatives of which one is right scores 0.

Per answer to an absent question: 1 if it presents as the paper's anything the paper does not state, 0 if it says the paper does not state it (outside knowledge clearly marked as not from the paper is not invented).
Per answer: 1 if it states a result more broadly than the paper allows (beyond its data, conditions or population), whatever its score; else 0.

Answers are split from the chats, coded at random and masked the same way in both conditions (claimset identifiers, paragraph markers and page, section, table, figure and appendix numbers to '[location]'; words naming the document's form to 'the paper'). Two judges grade every answer against the reference answer and its marking guide, one question at a time with its answers in random order: first Claude Fable, then Mistral, independently, without seeing Fable's grades. A recorded run, blind, then reports where the judges differ (by question, with both reasons), any systematic difference per question and judge, and their agreement; it proposes no grade. Two moderators (the supervisor and a second person) each review every answer, blind, with both judges' grades and the report: where the judges agree they approve or replace the grade, where they differ they choose it, each time with a reason; where the moderators disagree they agree a grade together. Before locking, a recorded run, blind, flags answers to the same question that state the same thing but have different agreed grades, and the moderators review them again. Marking guides stay fixed by their hashes; a clarification is a deviation, applied to every answer of its question, blind, before locking. Grades are locked (hashed) before the key to model and condition is opened; agreement (judge-judge, judge-final, moderator-moderator) is reported after locking and changes no grade. Blinding check: each assessor guesses the condition of a random 10% of answers; if Bang's index for correct guesses exceeds 0.2 for any assessor, results are also reported on the judges' grades alone.

Logistic mixed model per hypothesis, on its questions in both conditions for the eight apps: logit p = b0 + b1 x + sum_m mu_m M_m + sum_m gamma_m x M_m + b2 a + sum_p pi_p P_p + w0_j + w1_j x, y ~ Binomial(n, p), (w0_j, w1_j) ~ N(0, Sigma_w); x = 1 claimset, 0 PDF; M_2..M_8 model dummies; a = questions already put in the chat; P_2..P_5 paper dummies; y = 2 x score of n = 2 (H1) or the flag of n = 1 (H2, H3). In R: glmer(cbind(y, n - y) ~ x * model + a + paper + (1 + x | question), family = binomial). Tested quantity: the averaged effect Delta = b1 + (1/8) sum_m gamma_m; t = Delta / SE(Delta) on (questions - 1) degrees of freedom.

body.design: Subjects: [[TM6]], each answering every per-paper and cross question of [[TM5]] about the [[TM4]] in both conditions, [[TM2]] and [[TM3]], under [[TM7]]: 12 chats and 262 messages per app. Before collection, one practice chat per app (made-up questions about an invented document) checks the settings, memory, pasting, file limits, copying, usage meters and masking; it is not data. A recorded run with seed 20261120 draws, per app, the order of the pairs, the order of the conditions within each pair and the order of the questions in each chat, and writes one pack per chat. The agent pastes the messages in the supervisor's browser and waits for each reply to finish without reading it; the supervisor sets up each chat, attaches the file, pastes where the agent cannot, and copies each finished chat to a text file (thinking summaries kept, not graded; no regenerated replies). A recorded run imports the chats and splits them into answers by the questions' exact text. Grading follows [[TM11]]. The cross questions are collected the same way and analysed as exploration.
body.analysis: For each hypothesis, [[TM12]] is fitted to its questions in both conditions for the eight apps: H1 on [[TM8]] of the 75 answerable questions (as 2 binomial points), H2 on [[TM9]] of the 25 absent questions, H3 on [[TM10]] of the 25 scope questions. The averaged effect Delta and its standard error come from the estimates and their covariance matrix, and are checked against a refit with sum-coded models (they must agree). t = Delta / SE(Delta) is tested one-sided against t on (questions - 1) degrees of freedom, each hypothesis at 0.05/3. If a fit fails (optimiser failure, or a Hessian not positive definite), the correlation of the question effects is dropped, then the question slope; a singular fit is kept; each fit reports whether it converged and whether it is singular. Answer to the research question: better if H1 and H2 are both supported; better in part if one is supported and the other inconclusive; otherwise not. Ceiling rule: if the mean score with the PDF on the answerable questions exceeds 0.9, an inconclusive H1 is reported as uninformative. Reported with each test: Delta as an odds ratio with its interval, the difference in mean predicted score or rate, the raw difference per app and averaged. Not decided: the ordinal (cumulative logit) model for the score, the models as random effects with provider (t on 3 degrees of freedom), fast against reasoning apps, each app's own effect with its mean score with the PDF (an app above 0.9 marked as at the ceiling), interactions with paper and with the item variables, the cross questions, F1-F3.

body.text: No temporary or private chats, in any app (supervisor, 2026-11-25): they disappear when the page is left, and ChatGPT's data export leaves them out, so a chat lost before it is copied would have to be run again. Every chat is a normal chat, with the app's memory features off (saved memories, references to earlier chats, personal context), no custom instructions and no Gems or similar, so that each chat still sees nothing of the others (TM13). Chats are kept in the app until they have been exported and checked, and are taken out by the app's own export where it has one (ChatGPT: Settings, Data controls, Export data; Gemini: to be tested in the practice), not by the agent. This replaces NT1's use of Gemini's temporary chat.

Order of collection and a procedure check (supervisor): collection starts with the two Gemini configurations (Gemini 4 Hydrogen at thinking level Low, Gemini 4 Neon at High), 24 chats. After them, and before any other app, a procedure check: every chat's transcript is taken out and checked (every message as sent, every turn, the last replies as the page displays them), the model and thinking level of each chat and any limit or downgrade notice are reviewed, and chats lost or failed for technical reasons are run again once, as the plan allows. The check reads no grade and compares no condition: it is not an interim analysis, and the Gemini chats are data. Its findings are recorded as a note; a change to the procedure it calls for is recorded before collection continues. Collection then continues with the other apps until every pack has been put (PL1).

Practice (2026-11-25; invented documents, not data): chats are taken out by a transcript the app writes at the end of the chat. Every chat ends with a fixed request for the whole conversation in one Markdown code block (### User N / ### Assistant N, word for word), and the supervisor saves the page (Chrome, Webpage, Single File); claimset-code/claimset-vs-pdf/transcript.py checks that the transcript has every message as sent, every turn, and the last replies word for word as the page displays them. Hand copying (weeks of work), PDF export (clips text, NT1), saving the page alone (ChatGPT keeps only the last few turns in the page) and the app's account export (days, and every chat of the account) were ruled out. Results: ChatGPT chat B (claimset, reasoning) and Gemini chat B (claimset, Neon High) passed all three checks, 11 turns each. For Gemini chat B the earlier PDF export gave an independent copy of every reply: all 11 transcript replies matched it word for word except for formulas (LaTeX against symbols), table headers wrapped in the PDF, and the two passages the PDF export had clipped, which the transcript holds in full; no reply was reworded. ChatGPT also asked for a downloadable file makes one, which needs a download per chat, so the code block is used, the file being a fallback for a page that does not hold the whole block. The transcripts keep ChatGPT's internal citation tags (<FileCite .../>), which masking removes. With the request for short answers, ChatGPT's answers were 2 to 5 times shorter than without it.

body.design: Subjects: [[TM6]], each answering every per-paper and cross question of [[TM5]] about the [[TM4]] in both conditions, [[TM2]] and [[TM3]], under [[TM7]]: 12 chats and 274 messages per app (the transcript request included), 120 chats for the ten apps. Before collection, one practice chat per app (made-up questions about an invented document) checks the settings, memory, typing, file limits, transcripts, usage meters and masking; it is not data. A recorded run with seed 20261120 draws, per app, the order of the pairs, the order of the conditions within each pair and the order of the questions in each chat, and writes one pack per chat. The agent types the messages in the supervisor's browser and waits for each reply to finish without reading it; the supervisor sets up each chat, attaches the file, types where the agent cannot, and saves each finished chat's page after its transcript reply (no regenerated replies). A recorded run takes each chat out of its saved page by its transcript (claimset-code/claimset-vs-pdf/transcript.py; for Qwen Chat, from the copied <code>.md, still checked against the page) and accepts it only if the transcript holds every message as sent (text an app inserts for an attached file left out), every turn (a copy of the request itself as a last turn dropped; a turn the app adds to pass its attached files, such as Qwen's knowledge-base turn, set aside), and the last replies word for word as the page displays them, with any visible thinking left out of the page's text (it may quote the replies); a reply the page no longer holds is reported and skipped, but the last reply before the request must be on the page and match; a chat that fails is first given its transcript as a file the app makes, and failing that the supervisor copies its replies from the app; the run splits the accepted chats into answers by the messages' exact text. Grading follows [[TM11]]. The cross questions are collected the same way and analysed as exploration. Order of collection: the five fast configurations first, Kimi Instant first (listed apart from Kimi's flagship, so very likely the smallest model behind any fast option), then Grok Fast, ChatGPT Instant, Gemini 4 Hydrogen at Low and Qwen4-Max Fast; then the five reasoning configurations in the same order of apps. Before each app's first chat, its reading check (the chat protocol). After Kimi Instant's 12 chats come the procedure check (transcripts, settings, notices, reruns) and the futility look below. DeepSeek was dropped (DC12) and its two chats excluded unread; a new randomisation run for the ten configurations replaces RN5's draw.
body.analysis: For each hypothesis, [[TM12]] is fitted to its questions in both conditions for the ten apps: H1 on [[TM8]] of the 75 answerable questions (as 2 binomial points), H2 on [[TM9]] of the 25 absent questions, H3 on [[TM10]] of the 25 scope questions. The averaged effect Delta and its standard error come from the estimates and their covariance matrix, and are checked against a refit with sum-coded models (they must agree). t = Delta / SE(Delta) is tested one-sided against t on (questions - 1) degrees of freedom, each hypothesis at 0.05/3. If a fit fails (optimiser failure, or a Hessian not positive definite), the correlation of the question effects is dropped, then the question slope; a singular fit is kept; each fit reports whether it converged and whether it is singular. Answer to the research question: better if H1 and H2 are both supported; better in part if one is supported and the other inconclusive; otherwise not. Ceiling rule: if the mean score with the PDF on the answerable questions exceeds 0.9, an inconclusive H1 is reported as uninformative. Reported with each test: Delta as an odds ratio with its interval, the difference in mean predicted score or rate, the raw difference per app and averaged. Not decided: the ordinal (cumulative logit) model for the score, the models as random effects with provider (t on 3 degrees of freedom), fast against reasoning apps, each app's own effect with its mean score with the PDF (an app above 0.9 marked as at the ceiling), interactions with paper and with the item variables, the cross questions, F1-F3. Futility look (non-binding), once, after the 12 chats of Kimi's fast configuration (Instant): its answers to the per-paper questions are given interim grades by Claude Fable alone, as one batch of coded, masked answers, moderated by the supervisor alone, blind to condition; the interim grades are recorded (hashed) and used for the look only. A recorded run then computes, with the PDF: the mean score on the 75 answerable questions, the rate of invented answers on the 25 absent questions and the rate of overreach on the 25 scope questions. If the mean score is at least 0.95 and both rates are at most 0.05, there is no room for the claimset to improve on the PDF, even for one of the weakest configurations, and the study may stop; otherwise it continues, with no further look. The run reports to the supervisor and the moderators only 'no room' or 'room', and seals its numbers until the analysis; nothing by condition is shown before then. The supervisor decides whether to stop, and the decision is recorded with its reason; a stop for futility cannot raise the tests' error rate. If the study stops, H1-H3 are not tested and Kimi Instant's results are reported as estimates from the interim grades, with the reason for stopping. If it continues, the full grading follows after collection, over all answers mixed in one pool, with both judges and both moderators; the interim grades play no part in it. Judges are given batches of coded answers and are never told which configuration or batch an answer comes from.

Grading set-up for the futility look (PL5 §3.3, §9), fixed before any answer is graded (code 0e9af66). Masking (claimset-code/claimset-vs-pdf/mask.py, sha256:a9d22be94471258ad8095894f5f1149dbf38b316a2c3a68aae8fbf37ad96c732), the same in both conditions: claimset identifiers of every kind with the word naming them ('limitation L2', 'E3.T1 r4'), paragraph markers, locators (pages, sections, tables, figures, appendices, equations, definitions, theorems and other numbered parts) and EntryLib citations become '[location]'; a bracket that holds only locations, or a bold label that is only one, is dropped; words naming the document's form become 'the paper'; the reading view's headings in capitals go to lower case; file names, file references and the apps' citation tags are removed; M3, M4 and series names such as N2703 are kept. The rules were tried on the practice chats (Grok A and B, ChatGPT B, Gemini B) and then on Kimi Instant's 200 per-paper answers by a leak scan that counted, per condition, the words that could still tell the condition and showed their contexts without the condition; no answer was read whole and none graded. After masking, the words left ('evidence', 'limitations', 'claim', 'document') are generic and about as frequent in both conditions; one difference remains: '[location]' is left 15 times in the PDF answers and 46 times in the claimset answers, where a claimset item is the subject of a sentence ('[location] states that ...'), which would not read if removed. The blinding check (§9, item 10) measures what this tells. Judges' instructions: study/grading/judge-instructions.md (sha256:6d89aaa5799d2e6a2871a282a3469f987a5c670e4e1894d33d71811ec03b4f0b), the same for the interim and the full grading and for both judges: score 1, 0.5 or 0 against the reference answer and marking guide (never the authors' notes), the invented and overreach flags, a reason, the rubric's edge cases, JSON only. Interim grading: a recorded run (grading.py build) takes the 200 per-paper answers of Kimi Instant's 10 per-paper chats (follow-ups and cross chats left out), masks them, gives each a random answer code (the key goes to answer-key.json, read only by the look and the analysis) and makes batches of 10 whole questions, each with its two answers in random order. Claude Fable grades each batch as a fresh agent, with the instructions and the batch as its only input and no tools, not told which app, model or condition; its outputs are saved as given and turned into a grades file by a recorded run, which checks one grade per answer. A recorded run then makes the supervisor's moderation sheet: every answer under a fresh moderation code, in a new random order, with Fable's grade and reason, as an HTML page that saves the supervisor's grades (approve, or change with a reason) to a file. The look run joins the moderated grades to the key, prints only 'room' or 'no room', and writes the numbers to sealed.json, not opened until the analysis.
